found.why: Asks what ראש לנסיון in BR 59:6 means and why Joshua is 'head' of Ephraim's kingship; answers that Abraham, Joshua and David are 'samples' of what God will raise later — Joshua and David prefigure the two Mashiachs of Ephraim and Judah. Same Midrash, same question, and the same Mashiach ben Yosef/ben David resolution as Rav Tzadok's close.

No tzaddik truly dies; the past days of David and Abraham (והמלך דוד זקן בא בימים / ואברהם זקן בא בימים) remain 'alive and enduring'. Links the two verses of the haftarah and parashah to the living permanence Rav Tzadok reads in דוד מלך ישראל חי וקיים.
Because David broke his sleep for God, even his sleep has life: 'דוד מלך ישראל חי וקיים ומותא לא שריא עליו'. Parallels Rav Tzadok's claim that David never died but only sleeps for a time.

Maharal on the same Midrash (זקן שקנה שני עולמים; בפילון מפולש): the 'open gateway' is the straight, unswerving path to the World to Come, aligned with the Yud. Gives the sense of the phrase Rav Tzadok cites for Abraham's refinement to the supernal days.

footnotes.text:
**Agra DeKala, Chayei Sara 9** (Chassidus) — R. Tzvi Elimelech of Dinov asks what ראש לנסיון means and why Joshua is singled out as head of Ephraim's kingship. He reads נסיון as a sample: Abraham, Joshua and David show in advance what God will establish later, Joshua and David prefiguring the two Mashiachs. This is the same resolution Rav Tzadok reaches in his close on Mashiach ben Yosef and Mashiach ben David.
והנה השי"ת עתיד להעמיד תרין משיחין מאפרים ומיהודה, והראה דוגמתן ביהושע ודוד

**Yismach Moshe, Vayechi 1:3** (Chassidus) — R. Moshe Teitelbaum holds that death does not truly apply to a tzaddik, and that the days of David and Abraham, of whom בא בימים is written, are still alive. Like Rav Tzadok, he reads the shared phrase of the haftarah and the parashah as permanence of life.
ואי קאי על ימים העוברים, הא הם חיים וקיימים, כמו דכתיב (מלכים א' א א) והמלך דוד זקן בא בימים

**Yismach Moshe, Beshalach 16:3** (Chassidus) — Whoever breaks a natural force for God's honor gives life even to that force. So whoever breaks his sleep for God has life even while he sleeps, and therefore death has no hold on David. This parallels Rav Tzadok's David, who did not die but only sleeps for a time.
על כן דוד מלך ישראל חי וקיים (ר"ה כ"ה ע"א), ומותא לא שריא עליו

**Maharal, Derekh Chayyim 3:18** (Machshava) — The Maharal discusses the same Midrash: פילון means a straight, open place. The World to Come has a straight path that turns neither right nor left, the narrow path facing the Yud. This explains the phrase Rav Tzadok quotes for Abraham's refinement in the supernal days.
הרי לך כי עולם הבא יש לו דרך ישר, אשר אינו נוטה לימין ולשמאל, והוא הדרך שמגיע לחיי עולם הבא
